visual.subtitulo: From organism to biosphere, in depth

turnos.t: Let's start Topic 2 properly, with subtopic 2.
1: individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems.
First, the levels of organisation, the factors that decide where each species lives, the interactions between species, and the difference between habitat and niche.
Then, how a population grows: the J and S curves, carrying capacity and limiting factors.
And we finish with the human population, keystone species and human impact.
I'll give you the exact definitions, the way the exam wants them, and at the end you'll see how to answer the typical questions.

visual.nota: Population = same species + same area + same time

turnos.t: Picture a snowshoe hare in a forest in Canada.
On its own, it's an organism.
All the hares in that forest form a population.
Add the lynx, the plants and the fungi, and you have a community.
Add the soil, the water and the climate, and it's an ecosystem.
And all the ecosystems together make up the biosphere.
Now the definitions.
Species: two individuals are members of the same species if they can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.
Careful, this doesn't work well for organisms that reproduce asexually.
Population: a group of organisms of the same species that live in a given geographical area.
The rule to remember: same species, same area, same time, and able to interbreed.
Community, also called a biocoenosis: a group of populations of two or more different species occupying the same geographical area at the same time.
Several species, same place, same time.
Ecosystem: a community of interdependent organisms and the physical environment they interact with.
And the biosphere is an ecological system composed of individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems.
Here's the example from class.
The Sahara is hot and dry: camels, scorpions, snakes, and plants adapted to the lack of water.
The moist forests of Cuba are warm and wet: the bee hummingbird, the Cuban trogon and tree ferns.
Different conditions, different communities.
So what decides who lives where? Factors.
Biotic factors are all the living or once-living components of an ecosystem: food, competitors, predators, pathogens and mutualistic partners.
By their role, they are producers, which make their own food; consumers, which eat plants or other animals; and decomposers, which break down dead remains.
Abiotic factors are all the chemical and physical parts of an ecosystem: temperature, light, water, pH, salinity, dissolved oxygen and soil texture.
Each species has a range of tolerance for each one.
Temperature controls metabolism and survival.
Light controls photosynthesis and seasonal rhythms.
Water and salinity affect osmoregulation.
And pH, oxygen and soil restrict which habitats are possible.
Interactions are biotic factors too.
Always ask yourself: who wins and who loses?
Predation: one species hunts, kills and feeds on another, like the lynx and the hare, or a Venus flytrap and insects.
Herbivory: one species feeds on the biomass of a plant, like a giraffe eating acacia leaves.
Parasitism: one species takes nutrients from another while harming it, like ticks or intestinal worms.
Disease: a pathogen makes the host deviate from its normal functioning, like avian influenza.
All of these are plus, minus.
Mutualism: both species benefit.
That's plus, plus.
The clownfish shelters in the sea anemone, and the anemone gets nutrients and cleaning in return.
And competition is minus, minus: both of them lose.

tarjetas.detalle: Intra: male deer for mates · Inter: lions and cheetahs for prey
Hares stay near cover and feed more cautiously
Abundance, distribution, food webs: ~10-year lynx–hare cycle

turnos.t: In competition, two organisms occupy the same niche, or a very similar one, and compete for limited resources: food, water, space or mates.
Intraspecific competition happens within the same species, like male deer competing for females.
Interspecific competition happens between different species, like lions and cheetahs hunting similar prey.
Every interaction has three kinds of consequences.
Behavioural: behaviour changes.
Hares stay close to cover and feed more cautiously.
Ecological: abundance, distribution and food webs change.
The lynx and the hare go up and down in cycles of about ten years.
Evolutionary: selective pressures favour advantageous inherited traits, like faster, better-camouflaged hares.
If you read the words generations and inherited, it's evolutionary.

puntos: Role and position in the environment

visual.veredicto: Two species may share a habitat while using different resources

turnos.t: Two words students mix up: habitat and niche.
The habitat is where a species lives: the natural environment in which a species lives, which provides the physical and biological resources the individuals need.
The niche is how it lives: the role a species plays and the position it holds in the environment.
It's also defined as the set of biotic and abiotic conditions and resources a population depends on.
That's why two species can share a habitat and still have different niches, like the birds in Activity 4: same place, different resources.
Here's a trick: the habitat is the address; the niche is the job.

visual.pie: Chthamalus barnacles live high on the shore: their realised niche

turnos.t: The niche comes in two versions.
Fundamental niche: the full range of biotic and abiotic conditions and resources in which a species could theoretically survive and reproduce.
That's what it could occupy if it were on its own.
Realised niche: the actual conditions and resources in which a species exists due to biotic interactions.
That's what it really occupies, and it's almost always narrower, because competition pushes it out of part of its range.
Look at these barnacles, called Chthamalus, stuck to the rock high up on the shore.
They could live further down, but they don't. Why not?
Because lower down lives another species, Semibalanus, which competes with them for space.
Joseph Connell tested this on a rocky shore in Scotland, in a study published in 1961.
He removed the Semibalanus from the lower zone, and the Chthamalus started surviving there.
Conclusion: Chthamalus is limited by competition, a biotic factor.
Semibalanus, on the other hand, is limited higher up by drying out when the tide goes out, an abiotic factor.
Semibalanus is the stronger competitor, so its realised niche is almost the same as its fundamental niche.
This is Activity 5.
The habitat of both species: the rocky intertidal shore.
The interaction: interspecific competition.
And for the three-mark question: define both niches using whereas, say the realised niche is narrower because of competition, and apply it to the barnacles.
